newsitem.title: UK: Tobacco leaves could provide hepatitis test.
newsitem.headline: Tobacco leaves could provide hepatitis test.

text.p: Crushed tobacco leaves could provide a cheap and efficient test for hepatitis, Japanese researchers were quoted as saying on Thursday.

The leaves can be genetically altered to produce antigens against hepatitis, New Scientist magazine reported. Antigens are particles produced by living bodies against invaders such as viruses and can be used to test for infection.
Eventually, plants could be manipulated to produce an edible vaccine against hepatitis, a widespread and sometimes deadly scourge, the researchers said.
Yoichiro Watanabe and colleagues at the University of Teikyo said they used tobacco because geneticists already know a lot about it.
They said 10 leaves from one of the plants contained enough antigen to test more than half a million people.
"All we have to do is cultivate the tobacco and crush the leaves," Watanabe told New Scientist.
Existing methods use bacteria or yeast as a growing medium for the virus, and can be expensive and unwieldy.
Research leader Yoshimi Okada said growing the antigen in tobacco plants would be much cheaper and would allow poor countries to launch screening programmes.
Watanabe said the method might even extend to growing an edible vaccine, perhaps in a tomato. "We hope that vaccination could then be possible by simply eating the plant," he said.
Hepatitis B, 100 times more infectious than the HIV virus that causes AIDS, kills two million people a year and is responsible for 80 percent of all cases of liver cancer.
